tier_reason: icedland/disas-bench README lists XED at 55.39 MB/s decode and 15.67 MB/s decode+format next to Capstone 14.02, Zydis and bddisasm; the harness is public (bench.py, make-all.sh, bench/xed/main.c and Makefile with -flto -O3, bench/cs) with gcc 10.3.0 and an i5-6600K stated, so the evidence itself is A. Verdict is downgrade because the headline win over Capstone does not hold in the upstream suite's newer runs.

corrections.claimed_speedup: icedland/disas-bench (2021, i5-6600K, gcc 10.3.0, LTO builds): decode only XED 55.39 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19 and bddisasm 35.48 MB/s (about 1.62x and 1.56x, derived from page data); decode+format XED 15.67 vs Capstone 14.02 MB/s (about 1.12x, derived from page data). The upstream athre0z/disas-bench charts (October 2025, no LTO, newer library versions) reverse the Capstone result: decode+format XED about 21 MB/s vs Capstone about 28 MB/s on a Ryzen 9 9950X (GCC 13.3) and about 20 vs 26 MB/s on an i9-13900K (GCC 14.2), so XED runs at about 0.76-0.77x of Capstone; decode only XED about 67 and 73 MB/s vs Zydis (full) about 50 and 57 MB/s (about 1.3x) but behind bddisasm (about 106 and 103 MB/s) and Zydis (min) (about 90 and 104 MB/s) (2025 values derived from page data: bar lengths read from the pixels of bench-amd.png and bench-intel.png against their axis ticks). XED is slower than iced, yaxpeax and diStorm in every table of both runs.
corrections.caveats: Weak and unstable win: the 2021 icedland run puts XED 1.12x ahead of Capstone in decode+format (derived), but the 2025 upstream athre0z/disas-bench runs on two newer CPUs put it about 0.77x of Capstone (slower), and bddisasm and Zydis (min) now decode faster than XED; only the decode-only lead over Zydis (full) holds in both runs (about 1.3-1.6x). XED sits mid-table or lower and is beaten by iced, yaxpeax and diStorm throughout. The 2021 shootout is run by the iced maintainers (a competitor) in a fork of athre0z/disas-bench; the 2025 runs are in the suite of a Zydis co-author; XED's own README makes no speed claim. The 2021 fork's bench/xed/main.c ignores xed_decode's error return (it formats and advances by the reported length even on invalid bytes); upstream later skips one byte per bad instruction and counts them. One timed run per library (one subprocess, clock() around the loop). Capstone cannot run decode-only, so no decode-only ratio against it. The 2021 build is decoder-only (mfile.py --no-encoder) with -flto; the 2025 build uses neither.

notes: 2021 numbers match the icedland/disas-bench README rows exactly and the harness is A-grade, but the upstream athre0z/disas-bench October 2025 charts (Ryzen 9 9950X and i9-13900K) show XED slower than Capstone in decode+format (about 0.77x), so the claim against the incumbent is overstated; claimed_speedup and caveats rewritten. Metadata confirmed on github.com: Apache-2.0, 1.6k stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-08-24 (External Release v2026.08.23), active. Shortcomings: win over Capstone does not reproduce on newer runs, mid-table speed, competitor-run suites, single-run timings.

tier_reason: icedland/disas-bench README lists udis86 at 80.72 MB/s decode only and 12.02 MB/s decode+format next to Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48, XED 55.39 and Capstone 14.02; the harness is public (bench.py, make-all.sh, bench/udis86/main.c and Makefile with -O3, no LTO) with gcc 10.3.0 and an i5-6600K stated, run by a third party (the iced maintainers).

corrections.caveats: Loses to the incumbent: decode+format 12.02 MB/s is the slowest row of the table, below Capstone 14.02 (about 0.86x, derived from page data) and Zydis 22.24 MB/s; the win is decode-only against Zydis, bddisasm and XED, where Capstone cannot run. iced, yaxpeax and diStorm decode faster. Shootout run once per library by the iced maintainers (a competitor) in 2021; udis86 was later dropped from the upstream athre0z/disas-bench, so no newer run exists, and in that suite's 2025 runs on newer CPUs bddisasm (about 103-106 MB/s) and Zydis (min) (about 90-104 MB/s) decode much faster than in 2021, so the decode-only lead is a 2021 snapshot. udis86 was built without LTO (library and bench) while the others used -flto, which handicaps udis86 rather than helping it. Narrower ISA coverage: the README lists extensions up to SSE4.2/AES and decode.c has partial VEX but no EVEX/AVX-512 handling, so unsupported bytes are marked invalid; the bench does not count invalid instructions or check that rows decode the file the same way, and part of the decode-only lead may come from that narrower coverage. Last commit December 2014 (abandoned).

notes: Numbers match the icedland/disas-bench README rows exactly; tier A holds (public harness, gcc 10.3.0, flags in make-all.sh and bench/udis86/Makefile, i5-6600K). Metadata confirmed on github.com: BSD-2-Clause, 1.1k stars, not archived, last commit 2014-12-25 (abandoned). Shortcomings: slower than Capstone in decode+format, decode-only win only over Zydis/bddisasm/XED in a 2021 single-run snapshot, no AVX-512 coverage, abandoned since 2014.

tier_reason: First-party README chart (benchmark-time.svg, hyperfine means from scripts/benchmark-addr2line.sh, plotted by scripts/benchmark-plot.py) shows gimli addr2line faster than binutils addr2line, eu-addr2line and llvm-addr2line on four inputs; benchmark code is public but no CPU model, compiler or tool versions are stated (openSUSE Tumbleweed rolling image, unpinned), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Current benchmarks show a performance improvement in all cases'. Mean wall times read from the bar heights of benchmark-time.svg (derived from page data: bar geometry measured against the chart's 0.5 s axis ticks): libxul.so (162MB, 500 queries) gimli 0.10 s vs binutils addr2line 1.15 s (about 11x), llvm-addr2line 0.48 s (about 4.7x), eu-addr2line 3.25 s (about 32x); clangd-18 (360MB, 500 queries) 0.18 s vs binutils 2.92 s (about 16x), llvm 0.39 s (about 2.1x), eu 2.17 s (about 12x); mold (314MB, 1000 queries) 0.14 s vs binutils 1.19 s (about 8.5x), llvm 0.36 s (about 2.6x), eu 0.82 s (about 5.9x); postgres (38MB, 10000 queries) 0.067 s vs binutils 0.176 s (about 2.6x), llvm 0.079 s (about 1.2x), eu 1.91 s (about 28x). All ratios are approximate chart readings.
corrections.workload: Whole-command wall time (hyperfine mean) of 'addr2line -af -e <file>' resolving a fixed-seed random sample of addresses read from stdin, on four debug-info files: Firefox libxul.so.debug (162MB, 500 queries), clangd-18.debug (360MB, 500), mold.debug (314MB, 1000) and postgres.debug (38MB, 10000); each run includes process start-up and DWARF loading.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --features bin inside an opensuse/tumbleweed Docker image (scripts/docker/Dockerfile-opensuse installs rustup, binutils, elfutils, llvm and hyperfine unpinned) via scripts/benchmark-addr2line-docker.sh; baseline tools are the image's /usr/bin/addr2line, /usr/bin/llvm-addr2line and /usr/bin/eu-addr2line, versions not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party chart only: no numbers in text, no CPU model, tool versions float with the Tumbleweed image (SVG metadata dates the chart 2024-08-06), hyperfine --min-runs=1 so slow tools may be timed once or twice. Ratios above are read from SVG bar geometry, not from published values. Each run is a whole CLI invocation, so start-up and lazy DWARF parsing dominate at small query counts; the README itself says the library 'aims to perform similarly' to the existing tools. The address sample is generated by gimli addr2line itself (--all) and output equivalence across tools is not checked. Benchmark script and plotting script are public, so the chart can be regenerated.

notes: README claim and chart confirmed; I extracted approximate means from the SVG bars (gimli about 2.6-16x faster than binutils addr2line, 1.2-4.7x faster than llvm-addr2line) and added them as derived values. Tier C stays (first-party, no CPU or versions). Metadata confirmed on github.com: Apache-2.0 OR MIT, 429 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-08-01 (Release 0.27.1), active. Shortcomings: chart-only numbers, no hardware or tool versions, single-run minimum, CLI start-up included.
